propositions.text: The applicant is an offender serving an indeterminate sentence after designation as a dangerous offender, seeking judicial review of parole denial.
propositions.quote: The applicant is an offender serving an indeterminate sentence of imprisonment (following his designation as a dangerous offender) who seeks judicial review of the denial of his application for parole.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant is an offender serving an indeterminate sentence after designation as a dangerous offender, seeking judicial review of parole denial.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed for reasons set out below.
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out below, I have concluded that the present application should be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The application for judicial review is dismissed for reasons set out below.

propositions.text: The decision contains graphic descriptions of the applicant's crimes and sexual acts as a warning to readers.
propositions.quote: I wish to warn readers of this decision that it contains graphic descriptions of the applicant’s crimes and other acts of a sexual nature.

paragraphs.summary: The decision contains graphic descriptions of the applicant's crimes and sexual acts as a warning to readers.

propositions.text: Applicant's dangerous offender designation followed conviction on four counts of attempted sexual assault in 1989 (index offence).
propositions.quote: The applicant’s designation as a dangerous offender, and consequent indefinite imprisonment, followed his conviction on four counts of attempted sexual assault.

propositions.text: Index offence involved attempts to lure young girls into vehicle and police found various incriminating items in vehicle and home.
propositions.quote: It involved two separate attempts by the applicant in September 1989 to lure young girls into his vehicle. A police search of the applicant’s vehicle at the time found handcuffs, a knife, rope, a camera, paper towels, a ground sheet, pills in a container labelled “penis-enlarger”, a pair of girl’s panties and a teddy bear carrying a beach ball. A subsequent search of the applicant’s home found: A photo album containing pictures of young girls that appeared to have been taken in a public place; Nightgowns that would fit young girls; Clippings of newspaper advertisements requesting babysitters for young girls; A pornographic book about a girl’s first sexual experience; Documents the applicant had written, including: One detailing a plan to abduct two young girls called “A True Story”; Another entitled “Plans for the Future” containing stories of sexually assaulting little girls, a list of 65 schools in various towns, complete with the number of students and teachers in each school, the location of police detachments in the areas, a list of local motels, and a description of disguises and vehicles for use to commit these crimes; Another entitled “The Best Years of My Life, The First Trip” was a detailed story of abducting and murdering young girls that included the use of handcuffs, a knife and a camera.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's dangerous offender designation followed conviction on four counts of attempted sexual assault in 1989; police found incriminating items in vehicle and home.

propositions.text: Applicant's prior criminal history includes multiple offences from 1960 to 1980 with various sentences.
propositions.quote: The following table provides information concerning the applicant’s criminal history prior to the index offence: Date Offence Sentence November 7, 1960 Common Assault Suspended sentence, nine months’ probation July 29, 1963 Indecent Assault on Female Suspended sentence, 18 months’ probation October 26, 1964 Common Assault Three months definite, 18 months indefinite January 6, 1965 Breach of Recognizance Two years definite, two years indefinite March 18, 1969 Indecent Assault on Female, Possession of a Weapon, and Common Assault 10.5 years August 6, 1980 Possession of a Weapon Seven years and six months

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's prior criminal history includes multiple offences from 1960 to 1980 with various sentences.

propositions.text: Psychological report states applicant sexually assaulted or attempted to assault 17 girls aged 5-13 from age 17 to 50.
propositions.quote: According to a psychological/psychiatric assessment report dated July 20, 2015, that was referred to in the Parole Board of Canada’s decision, the applicant has acknowledged sexually assaulting or attempting to sexually assault 17 girls between the ages of 5 and 13 beginning when he was 17 years old and ending with his indefinite incarceration in 1989 (when he was 50 years old).

propositions.text: One victim was assaulted about 12 times; others were victimized once.
propositions.quote: With one exception, the girls were victimized only once. The exception was a 7-year-old neighbour of the applicant who was sexually assaulted about 12 times when he was 17 years old.

paragraphs.summary: Psychological report states applicant sexually assaulted or attempted to assault 17 girls aged 5-13 from age 17 to 50; one victim assaulted about 12 times.

propositions.text: Applicant acknowledged various acts including stealing girls' garments, obscene calls, forcing victims into car, molestation, masturbation, choking, threats with knife.
propositions.quote: The applicant has also acknowledged having: Stolen young girls’ garments, from clothes lines or by entering back doors of houses, for masturbatory purposes; Made obscene phone calls to young girls after obtaining phone numbers from babysitting advertisements; Offered rides to victims; Forced or dragged victims into his car, sometimes at knife point or using an imitation gun; Undressed or molested some of his victims; Masturbated in front of victims; Had his victims masturbate him; Choked one victim; Used a knife to force victims to comply with his wishes; Threatened to kill one victim if she continued screaming while he dragged her to his car.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant acknowledged various acts including stealing girls' garments, obscene calls, forcing victims into car, molestation, masturbation, choking, threats with knife.

propositions.text: Applicant has spent almost 50 years in prison, is 78, in poor health, uses wheelchair, claims no longer interested in young girls.
propositions.quote: Including the almost 28 years since being incarcerated indefinitely for his index offence, the applicant has spent almost 50 years of his life behind bars. He is now 78 years old and in poor health. He uses a wheelchair and suffers from a litany of ailments. He claims he has not fantasized about young girls for many years and is no longer interested in them.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant has spent almost 50 years in prison, is 78, in poor health, uses wheelchair, claims no longer interested in young girls.

propositions.text: Applicant is UK citizen, subject to Deportation Order since 1999, would be released to CBSA for removal to UK if granted parole.
propositions.quote: He is a citizen of the United Kingdom. Though he has lived in Canada since 1950, he never became a citizen of Canada. Because of his conviction for an offence punishable with a maximum term of imprisonment of ten years, he has been subject to a Deportation Order since 1999. Therefore, if the applicant is granted parole, he is to be released into the custody of Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA) for removal to the UK.

propositions.text: Applicant accepts deportation and wishes to return to UK, fearing he will die in prison first.
propositions.quote: The applicant accepts this. In fact, he has expressed a wish to return to his home country, as well as a concern that he will die in prison first.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant is UK citizen, subject to Deportation Order since 1999, would be released to CBSA for removal to UK if granted parole; applicant accepts and wishes to return.

propositions.text: Applicant requested transfer to England under International Transfer of Offenders Act; Canada and UK consented, applicant's consent pending.
propositions.quote: In November 2013 the applicant made a request under the International Transfer of Offenders Act, SC 2004, c 21, for transfer to England. Such a transfer would require the consent of Canada, of the UK and of the applicant. It appears that Canada and the UK have recently consented to the requested transfer. It remains only for the applicant to consent.

propositions.text: Parties agree application is not moot; circumstances differ if deported as parolee or transferred under the Act.
propositions.quote: Though it appears that the applicant now has a path to obtaining his stated goal of returning to his home country before he dies, the parties are agreed that the present application is not moot. It appears that the circumstances of the applicant’s return to the UK would be quite different if he were deported as a parolee as opposed to being transferred under International Transfer of Offenders Act.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant requested transfer to England under International Transfer of Offenders Act; Canada and UK consented, applicant's consent pending; parties agree application not moot.

propositions.text: Applicant has behaved well in prison, obeys rules, respectful, no criminal or gang activity, no substance abuse suspicion.
propositions.quote: It appears that the applicant has behaved well in prison. He obeys the rules, is respectful toward others and is not engaged in any criminal or gang activity. He is also not suspected of any substance abuse.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant has behaved well in prison, obeys rules, respectful, no criminal or gang activity, no substance abuse suspicion.

propositions.text: Applicant completed high intensity group therapy in 2001, did well, but refused further participation after 2009.
propositions.quote: In 2001 he completed a high intensity group therapy program as part of which he wrote a comprehensive crime cycle and relapse prevention plan. He did well in the program. However, having completed that program once, he could not repeat it, and was limited thereafter to maintenance programs. He participated in such programs until 2009, after which he refused further participation.

propositions.text: Applicant claims refusal due to loss of faith in further participation after 20 years and parole denials.
propositions.quote: He claims that, after serving 20 years of his indefinite sentence and being denied parole several times, he lost faith that further participation would be fruitful.

propositions.text: Applicant refused to be interviewed about refusal to participate in treatment.
propositions.quote: He also refused to be interviewed about his refusal to participate.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant completed therapy in 2001, refused further participation after 2009, claims loss of faith; refused interview about refusal.

propositions.text: Applicant participated in numerous Escorted Temporary Absences without incident and developed pro-social support network.
propositions.quote: The applicant has participated in numerous Escorted Temporary Absences from prison without incident, and has developed a pro-social support network.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant participated in numerous Escorted Temporary Absences without incident and developed pro-social support network.

propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of May 2, 2016 Appeal Division decision affirming October 21, 2015 Parole Board denial of parole.
propositions.quote: The applicant seeks judicial review of a May 2, 2016 decision of the Appeal Division of the Parole Board of Canada which affirmed an October 21, 2015 decision of the Parole Board denying the applicant’s application for parole.

propositions.text: The two tribunals are referred to as Appeal Division and PBC respectively.
propositions.quote: Hereinafter, these two tribunals will be referred to the Appeal Division and the PBC, respectively.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of May 2, 2016 Appeal Division decision affirming October 21, 2015 Parole Board denial of parole; tribunals named Appeal Division and PBC.

propositions.text: Appeal Division can reverse, cancel or vary PBC decision under s.147(4)(d) of Corrections and Conditional Release Act.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division had the power to reverse, cancel or vary the decision of the PBC: s. 147(4)(d) of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, SC 1992, c 20.

propositions.text: Appeal Division's grounds of appeal are essentially judicial review grounds (Cartier v Canada).
propositions.quote: the grounds of appeal listed in s. 147(1) are essentially those associated with judicial review: Cartier v Canada (Attorney General), 2002 FCA 384 at para 6 [Cartier].

propositions.text: On judicial review of Appeal Division's affirmation, court must ensure PBC's decision is lawful (Cartier).
propositions.quote: Where, as here, the Appeal Division has affirmed the PBC’s decision, the judge on judicial review of the Appeal Division’s decision is actually required ultimately to ensure that the PBC’s decision is lawful: Cartier at para 10.

propositions.text: It is necessary to look at both Appeal Division and PBC decisions.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, it is necessary to look at both decisions.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal Division can vary PBC decision; grounds are judicial review; court must ensure PBC decision lawful; both decisions must be reviewed.

propositions.text: Parole criteria in s.102 of Corrections and Conditional Release Act require no undue risk and reintegration contribution.
propositions.quote: The criteria for granting parole are set out in section 102 of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act: 102 The Board or a provincial parole board may grant parole to an offender if, in its opinion, (a) the offender will not, by reoffending, present an undue risk to society before the expiration according to law of the sentence the offender is serving; and (b) the release of the offender will contribute to the protection of society by facilitating the reintegration of the offender into society as a law-abiding citizen.

paragraphs.summary: Parole criteria in s.102 require no undue risk and reintegration contribution.

propositions.text: PBC summarized its task and pertinent details of applicant's history in its decision.
propositions.quote: The PBC began its decision by summarizing its task as well as some pertinent details of the applicant’s history.

paragraphs.summary: PBC summarized its task and pertinent details of applicant's history in its decision.

propositions.text: PBC considered increasing violence, premeditation, high risk factors, lack of insight, refusal of treatment, psychological assessments, lack of release plan.
propositions.quote: The PBC also made reference to certain information and reports that were considered in reaching its decision. In addition to some of the facts discussed above, these included: The increasing violence of the applicant’s offences over time; His offences were well thought-out in advance of actually committing them; Contributing risk factors identified by Correctional Service Canada (CSC) as requiring a high level of intervention, such as personal/emotional orientation and community functioning; Reports that the applicant has not displayed insight into his offences or crime cycle, and continues to minimize his offences, including stating that he “never hurt anybody” (apparently based on the fact that he never penetrated any of his victims); Because of his refusal to participate in further treatment programs, he is not considered engaged in his Correction Plan and his reintegration potential has been rated as low; Psychological assessments that have diagnosed the applicant as being sexually deviant, and showing traits of men who tend to reoffend sexually at a high rate, giving rise to a high risk to reoffend sexually despite his age and limited mobility, and necessitating significant coordination, information sharing and strict supervision if released; The applicant has not provided a release plan to address his need for strict supervision if released, and his relapse prevention plans are superficial;

paragraphs.summary: PBC considered increasing violence, premeditation, high risk factors, lack of insight, refusal of treatment, psychological assessments, lack of release plan.

propositions.text: PBC concluded negative factors outweigh positive; risk of reoffending remains undue; denied parole.
propositions.quote: After summarizing and balancing the positive and negative aspects of the applicant’s case, the PBC concluded that the latter outweigh the former, and the risk that the applicant will reoffend remains undue. The PBC denied parole on that basis.

paragraphs.summary: PBC concluded negative factors outweigh positive; risk of reoffending remains undue; denied parole.

propositions.text: Appeal Division can intervene only if PBC decision is unfounded or unreasonable; cannot substitute discretion.
propositions.quote: Based on its limited power, the Appeal Division indicated that it could intervene only where it found that the PBC’s decision was unfounded and unsupported by the information that was available at the time; it does not have the jurisdiction to substitute its discretion for that of the PBC unless the PBC’s decision was unreasonable or unfounded.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal Division can intervene only if PBC decision is unfounded or unreasonable; cannot substitute discretion.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division summarized the PBC's decision and applicant's arguments and found no grounds to intervene.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division summarized the analysis in the PBC’s decision and the applicant’s arguments, and concluded that there were no grounds for it to intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division summarized the PBC's decision and applicant's arguments and found no grounds to intervene.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division stated that 'undue risk to society' in s. 102 of the CCRA refers to any society, not just Canadian society.
propositions.quote: the Appeal Division stated that the concern for “an undue risk to society” and the effort to “contribute to the protection of society” in s. 102 of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act refer to any society rather than just Canadian society.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division concluded the PBC was correct to consider society in the UK where the applicant would be released.
propositions.quote: It concluded that the PBC was therefore correct to consider society in the UK where the applicant would be released.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division found 'undue risk to society' includes any society and upheld PBC's consideration of UK society for release.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division confirmed the PBC accurately summarized the applicant's criminal history and progress addressing risk factors.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division also confirmed that the PBC had accurately summarized the applicant’s criminal history and progress in addressing his risk factors.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found the PBC's conclusion that the sentence was tailored to meet the applicant's needs was reasonable.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division found that the PBC’s conclusion that the applicant’s sentence was being tailored to meet his needs was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division confirmed PBC's accurate summary of applicant's history and found sentence tailoring reasonable.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division summarized key conclusions of the Psychological Risk Assessment and noted CSC's low assessment of reintegration potential, motivation, and accountability.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division summarized the key conclusions of the relevant Psychological Risk Assessment, and noted CSC’s assessment of the applicant’s reintegration potential, motivation and level of accountability as low.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division summarized Psychological Risk Assessment and noted CSC's low assessment of applicant's reintegration potential.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found no merit in the specific points raised by the applicant's submission.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division also found no merit in the specific points raised in the applicant’s submission.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division found no merit in the applicant's specific submission points.

propositions.text: The applicant argues the Appeal Division's decision based on PBC findings was reviewable on various grounds including minimization of offences and improper reliance on reports.
propositions.quote: The applicant argues, on various grounds, that the Appeal Division’s decision, based as it was on the findings of the PBC, was reviewable. The following arguments are addressed in the analysis below: Erroneous conclusion that the applicant minimizes his offences and the harm caused thereby; Improper reliance on reports virtually copied from earlier reports; Improper focus on fictional stories of a sexual nature authored by the applicant long ago; Improper reliance on alleged acts for which the applicant was not convicted rather than his criminal record; Acting unfairly and beyond its jurisdiction in thwarting the applicant’s request and the CBSA’s efforts to return to him to the UK; Failure to contact authorities in the UK to make adequate arrangements for a deported parolee; Erroneous conclusion that the applicant could/would still lure young girls for sexual purposes; Improper reliance on the applicant’s refusal to participate in Sex Offender Maintenance Program; Erroneous conclusion that the applicant still has unaddressed needs; Improper use of the present perfect tense to suggest that the applicant’s acts in the long past continue to the present.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the Appeal Division's decision was reviewable on multiple grounds including minimization and improper reliance on reports.

propositions.text: The applicant argues his continued incarceration violates ss. 7, 12, 15 of the Charter and s. 2 of the Canadian Bill of Rights.
propositions.quote: The applicant also argues that his continued incarceration violates ss. 7, 12 and 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Part I of the Constitution Act, 1982, being Schedule B to the Canada Act 1982 (UK), 1982, c 11 [Charter], as well as s. 2 of the Canadian Bill of Rights, SC 1960, c 44.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues his continued incarceration violates Charter rights and the Canadian Bill of Rights.

propositions.text: Most alleged errors by the applicant are reviewed on a reasonableness standard; jurisdictional errors may be reviewed on correctness standard.
propositions.quote: For the most part, the errors alleged by the applicant are to be reviewed on a standard of reasonableness. This is certainly true of arguments by the applicant concerning the weight given to various issues and evidence related thereto. Though the applicant did not argue the point, I recognize that his argument that the PBC acted outside its jurisdiction or failed to perform its duty may be subject to review on a standard of correctness.

paragraphs.summary: The court states most alleged errors are reviewed for reasonableness; jurisdictional errors for correctness.

propositions.text: The PBC relied on applicant's statements denying penetration and claiming attempted assaults to conclude he minimized offences.
propositions.quote: The PBC appears to have relied on statements by the applicant that he never penetrated any of his victims as a basis for concluding that he minimized his offences. The PBC may also have reached this conclusion based in part on the applicant’s assertion that his index offence concerned mere attempted (not actual) sexual assaults.

paragraphs.summary: The PBC concluded the applicant minimized offences based on his statements denying penetration and claiming attempted assaults.

propositions.text: The applicant asserts he was stating facts and it was improper for PBC to characterize this as minimization.
propositions.quote: The applicant asserts that he was simply stating facts when he noted these things. The applicant argues that it was therefore improper for the PBC to characterize his statements as minimization of his offences.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues he was stating facts and PBC improperly characterized this as minimization.

propositions.text: Applicant's statements suggest he does not recognize seriousness of offences and thus minimized them.
propositions.quote: A person’s statements of mere facts during a discussion of their offences and the harm those offences have caused may, in context, reveal that the person does not recognize the seriousness of their offences. In the applicant’s case, his further statement that he “never hurt anybody” suggests just that. His repeated references to not having penetrated his victims and having merely attempted sexual assault in his index offence also suggest that he considers these facts to somehow excuse or lessen the severity of his offences.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds applicant's statements suggest minimization of offence seriousness.

propositions.text: Applicant's harm to victims included physical harm; mental harm can be more painful and enduring than physical harm.
propositions.quote: Firstly, since the applicant has acknowledged that he forced or dragged some of his victims, that he molested them, had them masturbate him, and choked one victim, it is difficult to understand any suggestion that harm to his victims was not physical. I can only think that the applicant’s concept of physical harm required some sort of permanent injury. I disagree. My second reaction to the idea that harm to the applicant’s victims was mainly mental is to note that mental harm, even though it is not visible, can be much more painful and enduring for the victim than any physical harm.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds applicant caused physical and mental harm, noting mental harm can be more painful and enduring.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel characterized assaults on a young girl as an 'affair' and 'ongoing relationship'.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s counsel characterized the series of interactions between that girl (who was 7 years old at the time) and the applicant (who was 17 at the time) as an “affair” and an “ongoing relationship”.

propositions.text: The court rejects characterization of relationship as an affair or consensual romantic relationship due to girl's age and lack of capacity to consent.
propositions.quote: I cannot accept the characterization of a relationship between a 17 year old boy and a young girl, whether she is 7 or 12, as an affair. The word “affair” suggests an ongoing consensual romantic relationship. However, a young girl obviously does not have the capacity to give the required consent.

propositions.text: The court rejects suggestion that romantic encounters happen at that young age regardless of girl's age.
propositions.quote: I also reject counsel’s suggestion that “romantic encounters do happen at that age”, again regardless of whether the girl was 7 or 12.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's counsel called assaults an 'affair'; court rejects this due to girl's age and lack of consent capacity.

propositions.text: The applicant has not shown it was unreasonable to conclude he minimized elements of his offending.
propositions.quote: The applicant has not convinced me that it was unreasonable to conclude that he minimized elements of his offending.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes it was reasonable to find the applicant minimized his offending.

propositions.text: The applicant complains that many portions of the PBC's report are copied from earlier reports, suggesting improper consideration.
propositions.quote: The applicant complains that many portions of the PBC’s report are essentially copied from earlier reports, presumably suggesting that the PBC did not properly consider the situation.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant complains the PBC's report copies earlier reports, implying improper consideration.

propositions.text: It is understandable that PBC's report contains similar passages as underlying facts are unchanged, so conclusions remain unchanged.
propositions.quote: In my view, it is understandable that the PBC’s report would contain many passages that are similar to, or even the same as, passages found in previous PBC reports. Most of the underlying facts appear to be unchanged, including the applicant’s index offence, his other criminal convictions, other acts he has acknowledged for which he was not convicted, and his unwillingness to participate in maintenance programs. To the extent that the relevant facts are unchanged, it is reasonable that the PBC’s conclusion would likewise remain unchanged.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable that PBC's report repeats passages due to unchanged facts and conclusions.

propositions.text: Without indication of error, reproducing portions of previous reports is not an error and avoids waste of effort.
propositions.quote: Without any indication that the PBC failed to consider the relevant facts, or misunderstood them, or applied them unreasonably, I am not prepared to find that the PBC erred in reproducing portions of its report from previous reports. To find otherwise would force the PBC to find different words for each report to say essentially the same things. This would be a waste of effort.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes reproducing report portions is not error and avoids waste without evidence of misunderstanding.

propositions.text: The applicant complains the PBC gives too much weight to his fictional stories written long ago.
propositions.quote: The applicant complains that the PBC makes too much of his stories, which are fictional and were written long ago.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant complains the PBC overemphasizes his old fictional stories.

propositions.text: The court is not convinced PBC misunderstood the fictional nature or age of stories and finds PBC's weight decision reasonable.
propositions.quote: Firstly, I am not convinced that the PBC misunderstood the fictional nature of the applicant’s stories or that they were written long ago. Also, it is for the PBC to decide on the weight that should be given to these stories. The fact that they are fictional and written long ago does not prevent the PBC from considering them. Moreover, the PBC mentions these stories only once in its decision. It does not appear that they were given undue weight.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PBC did not misunderstand the fictional stories and reasonably weighed them lightly.

propositions.text: The applicant argues he has freedom of thought and expression and should not be punished for writing fantasies.
propositions.quote: The applicant also argues that he has freedom of thought and of expression, that the writings in question were not criminal in any way, and that he should not be punished for writing such fantasy.

propositions.text: The respondent says the applicant is not punished for writing but writings are relevant to decision-making.
propositions.quote: The respondent counters that the applicant is not being punished for writing. This is not a matter of freedom of thought or of expression. Rather, the PBC included the applicant’s writings as a relevant consideration in its decision-making.

propositions.text: The court agrees it was not unreasonable for PBC to consider the applicant's disturbing writings.
propositions.quote: I agree. It was not unreasonable for the PBC to make reference to the applicant’s disturbing writings.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant claims freedom of expression; respondent says writings are relevant; court agrees PBC reasonably considered writings.

propositions.text: PBC gives too much weight to unconvicted sexual acts evidence against him
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the PBC gives “altogether too much weight” to evidence of acts of a sexual nature committed by him but for which he was never convicted.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues PBC gives too much weight to unconvicted sexual acts evidence against him.

propositions.text: PBC decides weight of evidence including admitted acts not in dispute
propositions.quote: it is for the PBC to decide on the weight that should be given to the evidence. The acts in question were admitted to by the applicant. The fact that the applicant committed these acts is not in dispute.

paragraphs.summary: Court states PBC decides weight of evidence including admitted acts not in dispute.

propositions.text: Unfair to encourage openness in therapy then hold acts against him; he should get credit for frankness
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that it is unfair to have encouraged him, as part of his participation in therapy programs, to be open about his past acts, and then to hold those acts against him later. The applicant argues that he should be given credit for his frankness.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues unfair to encourage openness in therapy then hold acts against him; he should get credit for frankness.

propositions.text: Applicant's honesty could be considered by PBC but it was not unreasonable to consider unconvicted sexual acts disclosed voluntarily
propositions.quote: I am not prepared to conclude that it was unreasonable for the PBC, as part of its decision-making, to consider acts of a sexual nature committed by the applicant, even if he were not convicted of any offence in respect of such acts, and even if those acts were disclosed voluntarily by the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds applicant's honesty could be considered but PBC reasonably considered unconvicted sexual acts disclosed voluntarily.

propositions.text: Highly prejudicial to use applicant's own statements against him
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that it was highly prejudicial to use the applicant’s own statements against him.

propositions.text: PBC reliance on undisputed acts was not prejudicial to applicant
propositions.quote: Given that the fact that the applicant committed these acts is not in dispute, I do not agree that the PBC’s reliance on them was prejudicial to the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues use of own statements was prejudicial; court disagrees as acts are undisputed.

propositions.text: PBC thwarted deportation efforts for 17 years by refusing parole, acting beyond or refusing jurisdiction
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that, for 17 years, the PBC has been thwarting efforts by him and by the Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA) to have him deported to the UK by refusing to grant him parole. The applicant argues that, in so doing, the PBC has acted beyond its jurisdiction and refused to exercise its jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Applicant quotes Appeal Division decision about CBSA unable to remove him due to indefinite custody
propositions.quote: In support of his position, the applicant quotes passages from the Appeal Division’s decision referring to the CBSA and the applicant’s request for an international transfer. These passages include the following: “The CBSA states that it had not been able to remove you from Canada under a deportation order because you were being held indefinitely in custody as a danger to the public as declared by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.”

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues PBC thwarted deportation for 17 years and acted beyond jurisdiction, citing Appeal Division passages.

propositions.text: Quoted passages do not support argument PBC wanted to thwart deportation; PBC fairly considered applicant's wish to return to UK
propositions.quote: nothing in the above-quoted passage, or the rest of the passages cited by the applicant, supports the argument that the PBC appeared to want to thwart the applicant’s deportation. In fact, from my reading of the PBC’s decision as a whole, I understand the PBC to have given fair consideration to the applicant’s wish to return to England, and to the requirements for granting that wish.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds quoted passages do not support PBC thwarting deportation; PBC fairly considered applicant's wish to return to UK.

propositions.text: PBC did not act outside jurisdiction by refusing parole and preventing deportation; removal order stayed until sentence completion under IRPA s.50(b)
propositions.quote: I do not accept that the PBC acted outside its jurisdiction when it prevented the applicant’s deportation by refusing to grant him parole. ... s. 50(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act ... makes it clear that a removal order against a foreign national sentenced to prison in Canada is stayed until the sentence is completed.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PBC did not act outside jurisdiction; removal order stayed until sentence completion under IRPA s.50(b).

propositions.text: PBC improperly assumed UK lacks adequate parole checks
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the PBC improperly assumed that the UK does not have adequate checks on parolees.

propositions.text: Disagrees with applicant; PBC reasonably concerned about losing control given responsibility for risk beyond Canada and applicant's offending history
propositions.quote: I disagree. I think the applicant was closer to the mark with an observation that the PBC does not want to lose control of the applicant. In my view, that is a reasonable concern for the PBC to have, given ... the PBC’s responsibility for the risk to society wherever it may be ... and the applicant’s history of offending while on release from detention.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues PBC wrongly assumed UK lacks parole checks; court finds PBC reasonably concerned about risk and control.

propositions.text: Unreasonable to expect applicant to build release plan; PBC had duty to facilitate by contacting UK authorities or pressuring parole officer
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that it was unreasonable to expect the applicant to come up with a release plan because (i) he is incarcerated, and (ii) his release would be in the UK. The applicant argues that the PBC had a duty to facilitate his building of a release plan by contacting authorities in the UK. The applicant urges that the PBC should at least have pressured the applicant’s parole officer to do so.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues PBC unreasonably expected him to build release plan and had duty to facilitate contacting UK authorities.

propositions.text: PBC's job is to consider parole application; no duty to build release plan
propositions.quote: The job of the PBC was to consider the applicant’s parole application. A release plan is a document that might be provided to the PBC as part of a parole application, but I have seen nothing to indicate that it is the PBC’s duty to work to build that plan.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PBC's job is to consider parole application; no duty to build release plan.

propositions.text: If PBC has no duty to facilitate release plan, then its protection duty does not extend to UK
propositions.quote: The applicant also argues that if the PBC has no duty to facilitate building a release plan in the UK, then it should follow that its concern for the protection of society does not extend to the UK.

propositions.text: Disagrees; society protection extends beyond Canada and duty scope is not tied to protection scope
propositions.quote: Firstly, as indicated above, the jurisprudence indicates that “society” is not limited to Canadian society. Secondly, I do not agree with the logic of tying the scope of the PBC’s duty to the scope of its concern for the protection of society.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues no duty means no protection duty beyond Canada; court disagrees, protection extends beyond Canada and duty scope differs.

propositions.text: Applicant is older, less healthy and less mobile than at index offence
propositions.quote: At 76 years old you are considerably older than you were when you committed the index offence. You have experienced a series of more or less significant health issues since 2001 and are not as mobile or as healthy as you were when you began to serve your sentence.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found applicant older, less healthy and less mobile than at index offence.

propositions.text: Applicant adds he is confined to a wheelchair
propositions.quote: The applicant adds that he is confined to a wheelchair.

propositions.text: PBC concluded applicant remains high risk to offend
propositions.quote: However, the PBC concluded that the applicant remained a high risk to offend.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant states he is wheelchair-bound; PBC concluded he remains high risk to offend.

propositions.text: Unreasonable to think wheelchair-bound man could commit sexual offenses; PBC uses double standard on health and past acts
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that it is unreasonable to conclude that a wheelchair-bound man could commit sexual offenses of the kind the PBC is concerned about. Among other things, the applicant argues that the PBC employs a double standard in that it dismisses his health problems that are in the past, but dwells on his sexual acts that have not occurred for several decades.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues it is unreasonable to think wheelchair-bound man could offend and PBC uses double standard on health and past acts.

propositions.text: No double standard; reasonable to consider past acts and current health affecting ability to offend
propositions.quote: I do not accept this “double standard” argument. I see nothing unreasonable in considering whether past acts by the applicant (even long past acts) might happen again, and also not considering health problems that do not currently affect the applicant’s ability to commit such acts.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects double standard argument; finds it reasonable to consider past acts and current health.

propositions.text: PBC's conclusion applicant remains high risk to offend was reasonable despite age and health
propositions.quote: Despite the applicant’s arguments, I am of the view that the PBC’s conclusion that he remains a high risk to offend was reasonable. He may be older and less physically able than he was, but he remains able to lure children.

propositions.text: Applicant claims no longer has urges; PBC considered those claims
propositions.quote: He claims that he no longer has the urges that led him to commit the sexual acts that concerned the PBC, but the PBC considered those claims.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PBC reasonably concluded applicant remains high risk; PBC considered applicant's claim of no urges.

propositions.text: Refusal to participate in maintenance therapy should not be held against him; he gave up after 20 years and parole denials
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that his refusal to participate in maintenance programs concerning his therapy should not be held against him. ... he participated actively ... until 2009 ... after ... being denied parole several times, he essentially gave up believing further participation would help.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues refusal to participate in maintenance therapy should not be held against him due to loss of hope after parole denials.

propositions.text: Explanation may or may not have been given to PBC; refusal to participate was reasonably of concern
propositions.quote: This is an explanation that may or may not have been given to the PBC in explaining his refusal to participate in maintenance programs. However, either way, I am not prepared to find that it was unreasonable for the PBC to conclude that, despite the applicant’s explanation, his continued refusal was of concern.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds refusal to participate was reasonably of concern regardless of explanation given to PBC.

propositions.text: PBC stated applicant has unaddressed needs from most recent program
propositions.quote: The most recent program you completed indicated that you still have a number of unaddressed needs.

propositions.text: PBC failed to identify these unaddressed needs
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the PBC failed to identify these unaddressed needs.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found applicant has unaddressed needs; applicant argues PBC failed to identify them.

propositions.text: The PBC’s decision cites several examples of the applicant’s unaddressed needs, including superficial relapse prevention plans.
propositions.quote: The PBC’s decision cites several examples of the applicant’s unaddressed needs, including the superficial nature of his plans to prevent his relapse.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the PBC cited several examples of the applicant's unaddressed needs, including superficial relapse prevention plans.

propositions.text: The applicant challenges the PBC decision consistent with Steele, but expands little on this at hearing.
propositions.quote: The Parole Board of Canada decision is being challenged consistent with Warden of Mountain Institution v. Steele, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1385 [(Steele)].

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the PBC decision is challenged consistent with Steele but offers little expansion at hearing.

propositions.text: Steele clarified parole assessment requirements and involved an indeterminate sentence prisoner.
propositions.quote: Steele clarified requirements for proper assessment of parole applications. As in the present case, it concerned a prisoner who was serving an indeterminate sentence.

propositions.text: In Steele, parole was denied despite submissions received; here, submissions were received and considered.
propositions.quote: In Steele, parole was denied despite, not because of, submissions that were received by the National Parole Board (as it was called then). That is not the case here.

propositions.text: Supreme Court found disciplinary breaches in Steele were explicable and insufficient to deny parole; here, PBC decision was not based on disciplinary breaches.
propositions.quote: Also, the Supreme Court found that disciplinary breaches that swayed the Board were explicable and not sufficient to deny parole. In the present case, the PBC’s decision was not based on disciplinary breaches.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Steele clarified parole assessment, differed from this case as submissions were considered here, and disciplinary breaches were not basis for denial here.

propositions.text: The court is not convinced the PBC failed to follow Steele instructions in this case.
propositions.quote: I am not convinced that, in the present case, the PBC failed to heed the instructions in Steele.

paragraphs.summary: The court is not convinced the PBC failed to follow Steele instructions in this case.

propositions.text: Applicant argues PBC’s use of present perfect tense improperly suggests ongoing offending.
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the PBC’s use of the present perfect tense in its decision improperly suggests that the applicant continues to commit the acts referred to.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the PBC’s use of present perfect tense improperly suggests ongoing offending.

propositions.text: Only one example of present perfect tense found in PBC decision, other cited examples were from different documents.
propositions.quote: The only example of this that I have found in the PBC’s decision is the following passage at page 4: “your predatory behaviour and deviant sexual attraction to female children is long standing and has spanned over 60 years of your life” (emphasis added).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds only one example of present perfect tense in PBC decision; other examples cited were from other documents.

propositions.text: Applicant argues it is untrue his criminal history spans 60 years since incarcerated since 1989 with no criminal activity in prison.
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that it is untrue that the applicant’s criminal history has spanned 60 years of his life, since he has been in prison since 1989, and there is no indication of any criminal activity by him while incarcerated.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues it is untrue his criminal history spans 60 years since incarceration in 1989 with no prison criminal activity.

propositions.text: Court satisfied PBC understood no sexual offenses since incarceration and use of present perfect tense was not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: While the applicant is factually correct, I am satisfied that the PBC did not misunderstand the fact that the applicant has not committed a sexual offense since he was incarcerated in 1989. In fact, the PBC noted his generally appropriate behaviour during that time. I am also satisfied that there was nothing unreasonable in the PBC’s use of the present perfect tense.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PBC understood no offenses since incarceration and its use of present perfect tense was reasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant argues PBC decision violated rights under ss. 7, 12, 15 of Charter and s. 2 of Canadian Bill of Rights.
propositions.quote: the applicant argues that his rights under ss. 7, 12 and 15 of the Charter, as well as s. 2 of the Canadian Bill of Rights, have been violated by the PBC’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the PBC decision violated his Charter and Canadian Bill of Rights rights.

propositions.text: PBC acknowledged applicant’s file was challenging due to dangerous offender and deportation status.
propositions.quote: the PBC acknowledged during the hearing of his parole application that his was a challenging file, “and not least because you are both a dangerous offender and a deportation case.”

propositions.text: PBC stated some interventions available to other offenders are effectively closed to applicant.
propositions.quote: These things make it particularly challenging for the board, because for all practical purposes, I think it’s fair to say that some of the interventions that are open to other offenders, are effectively closed off to you.

paragraphs.summary: The PBC acknowledged the applicant’s file was challenging due to dangerous offender and deportation status, limiting available interventions.

propositions.text: Applicant’s Charter and Bill of Rights arguments are superficial, citing no jurisprudence and little beyond quoting provisions.
propositions.quote: Unfortunately, the applicant’s arguments on these issues are superficial. The applicant cites no jurisprudence and, beyond citing the PBC’s comments in the preceding paragraph and the applicant’s situation as a foreign national, the applicant does little more than quote the relevant provisions of the Charter and the Canadian Bill of Rights.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant’s Charter and Bill of Rights arguments superficial and lacking jurisprudence.

propositions.text: Court not convinced any rights violation occurred; applicant remains imprisoned under valid indefinite sentence; PBC decision not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I will say that I am not convinced that there has been any violation of the applicant’s rights. The applicant remains in prison due to an indefinite sentence whose validity is not in issue. I have not found any aspect of the PBC’s decision to be unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court is not convinced any rights violation occurred and finds the PBC decision reasonable.

propositions.text: Court disagrees that applicant’s deportation status entitles him to parole; PBC’s concern for public protection is critical despite complications.
propositions.quote: I am unable to agree that the complicating fact of the applicant’s situation as a “deportation case” is sufficient to entitle him to parole. The PBC’s concern for the protection of society must be considered a critically important consideration in deciding the applicant’s parole application, even if his situation is complicated by his impending deportation.

propositions.text: Applicant’s situation challenges are not insurmountable.
propositions.quote: The challenges of the applicant’s situation are not insurmountable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds deportation status does not entitle applicant to parole and challenges are not insurmountable.

propositions.text: Applicant argues PBC decision causes arbitrary exile violating Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2.
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the PBC’s decision subjects him to arbitrary exile from his home country.

propositions.text: Court finds applicant’s exile difficulties are arbitrary only if PBC decision is unreasonable, which it is not.
propositions.quote: In my view, the applicant’s difficulties in returning to the UK can only be characterized as arbitrary to the extent that some aspect of the PBC’s decision can be characterized as unreasonable. As I have indicated, I have found no aspect of the PBC’s decision to be unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues arbitrary exile violates rights; court finds exile arbitrary only if PBC decision unreasonable, which it is not.

propositions.text: The application is dismissed with costs.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, the present application should be dismissed with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application with costs.
